results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?

For example, a 5/5 creature with trample and deathtouch blocked by a 3/3 creature can assign 1 damage to the blocker (lethal due to deathtouch) and 4 damage to the defending player. This works regardless of the blocker's toughness, because deathtouch makes any positive amount of damage lethal (rule 702.2c). The deathtouch rules function no matter what zone the damage comes from (rule 702.2d), and multiple instances of either ability are redundant (rules 702.2f, 702.19g). If the creature also has trample over planeswalkers, after assigning lethal damage to blockers and at least the planeswalker's loyalty in damage, further excess can be assigned to the planeswalker's controller (rule 702.19c).

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you are already at your maximum hand size. results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?

Specifically, if you are required to draw a card from an empty library, you attempt to draw, fail to draw any card (because there are none), and then the state-based action in [704.5b] checks that you attempted to draw from an empty library since the last check, causing you to lose the game. This applies whether the draw is a turn-based action (like the draw step draw) or the result of a spell or ability. If an effect replaces the draw (e.g., with a different action), the replacement is applied first per [121.6a] and [614.11], and if the replacement successfully avoids the draw attempt, you do not lose. If the effect merely offers a choice to draw (e.g., "you may draw a card"), you may choose to do so even from an empty library per [121.3], and if you do, you will lose as above. If an effect moves cards from your library to your hand without using the word "draw" (e.g., "put the top card of your library into your hand"), that is not a draw per [121.5], so you do not lose from an empty library; instead, per [609.3], the effect does as much as possible, which is nothing if the library is empty. The answer is the same for two-player and multiplayer games, as the relevant rules do not distinguish between player counts.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text: The combat phase has five steps in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat (rule [506.1]). As the defending player, you receive priority during each step after turn-based actions are completed and the active player passes priority. Specifically: during the beginning of combat step, after the active player chooses a defending player (if applicable, rule [507.1]) and both players pass priority, you get priority when the active player passes (rule [117.1]). During the declare attackers step, after attackers are declared and the active player passes priority, you get priority. During the declare blockers step, after you declare blockers (rule [509.1]) and the active player passes priority, you get priority. During the combat damage step, after combat damage is assigned and dealt (rules [510.1], [510.2]) and the active player passes priority, you get priority. During the end of combat step, the active player gets priority first (rule [511.1]), then you get priority after they pass. This answer assumes a two-player game; in multiplayer games with multiple defending players (e.g., rule [802.2]), priority order follows APNAP (active player, then each nonactive player in turn order).

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text: Layers are a system used to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to objects in Magic: The Gathering. The game applies effects in a specific sequence of layers (and sublayers within some layers) to ensure a consistent result. The layers are applied in the following order: Layer 1 (copiable values, including copy effects and merge effects), Layer 2 (control-changing effects), Layer 3 (text-changing effects), Layer 4 (type-changing effects, including card type, subtype, and supertype), Layer 5 (color-changing effects), Layer 6 (ability-adding or ability-removing effects), and Layer 7 (power- and toughness-changing effects, which has its own sublayers: 7a for characteristic-defining abilities, 7b for effects that set power and toughness to a specific value, and 7c for effects that modify power and toughness without setting them). Within each layer or sublayer, effects are generally applied in timestamp order (earlier effects first), unless a dependency relationship exists (rule 613.8), which overrides timestamps. If an effect applies in multiple layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer; for example, an effect that says 'This creature gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice' applies the color change in layer 5 and the +1/+1 in layer 7c (rule 613.6). The game continuously and automatically applies these layers to determine an object's final characteristics (rule 613.5). For example, a 2/2 black creature that becomes white (layer 5) and then gets +1/+1 from Honor of the Pure (layer 7c) becomes 3/3; if its color later changes to red (layer 5), Honor of the Pure's effect stops applying, and it returns to 2/2 (rule 613.5). Another example: a 2/2 creature with a +1/+1 counter (layer 7c) that gets +4/+4 from a spell (layer 7c) and +0/+2 from an enchantment (layer 7c) becomes 7/9; if an effect then sets it to 0/1 (layer 7b), it becomes 5/8 (0/1 base, plus +4/+4, +0/+2, and +1/+1 from the counter) (rule 613.5). The provided rules do not specify how this differs in multiplayer versus two-player games, so this answer applies to the two-player case; a multiplayer table may follow different rules not provided here.

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype. If a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. This is defined in rule 704.5j. The rule applies to all legendary permanents, including legendary creatures, planeswalkers (which now have the legendary supertype per rule 306.4), and any other permanent with the legendary supertype. It does not apply to legendary instants or sorceries, which are subject to a casting restriction instead (rule 205.4e). The rule is checked as a state-based action, meaning it is applied whenever a player would receive priority, and it is not a triggered ability or a spell. For example, if you control two copies of the legendary creature "Jace, Vryn's Prodigy" (assuming they have the same name), you must put one into its owner's graveyard. The legend rule is independent of card types or subtypes; changing an object's card types or subtypes does not change its supertypes (rule 205.4b). In the Commander variant, the legend rule still applies normally (rule 903.1), but note that the commander designation does not override the legend rule—if you control two legendary permanents with the same name, one must be put into the graveyard even if one is your commander. The legend rule also applies to legendary tokens (rule 111.9). The answer provided is for a two-player game; in multiplayer games with more than two players, the legend rule works the same way—each player individually checks their own permanents and applies the rule if they control two or more legendary permanents with the same name. No additional rules for multiplayer are needed beyond the standard state-based action.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: Your creature dies as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked, which occurs immediately before a player would receive priority. Specifically, after lethal damage is marked on the creature (whether from combat or a spell like Lightning Bolt), the game checks state-based actions. If the total damage marked on the creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, the creature is destroyed as a state-based action per rule 704.5g. This happens before any player gets priority to cast spells or activate abilities. For example, after Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to a 2/2 creature, the creature is destroyed as a state-based action before any player can respond (see rule 120.5). If the damage is dealt during combat, all combat damage is dealt simultaneously (rule 703.4m), and state-based actions are checked after that damage is dealt, before priority is given. The creature does not die immediately upon damage being marked; it dies during the next state-based action check, which occurs as part of the priority system (rule 117.5). Damage marked on the creature remains until the cleanup step (rule 120.6), but the creature will be destroyed by state-based actions well before then if lethal damage is marked. If an effect ends the turn (rule 724.1c), state-based actions are checked as part of that process, so the creature would die then as well. This answer assumes a two-player game; in multiplayer, the same rules apply regarding state-based actions and priority, but the turn order and defending player choices may differ—however, the timing of the creature's death remains the same.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: During the cleanup step, the following occurs in order: First, if the active player's hand has more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard down to that number [703.4n][514.1]. Normally, no player gets priority during the cleanup step [514.3], so no spells can be cast or abilities activated. However, if after the turn-based actions any state-based actions would be performed or triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack (including those that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"), those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, and the active player gets priority [514.3a]. Players may then cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins [514.3a]. If no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, the step ends without any player receiving priority [704.3][500.3]. If an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins [724.1d].

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is a triggered ability created by the resolution of a spell or ability, by a replacement effect, or by a static ability that allows a player to take an action. For example, the Earthbend keyword action (rule 701.66a) creates a delayed triggered ability that says "When that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control." This ability is created during the resolution of the Earthbend action and triggers later when the land dies or is exiled. Delayed triggered abilities are governed by rule 603.7 and its subrules, which cover how they are created, their source and controller, and how they interact with objects that change zones or characteristics.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instant and sorcery spells) can have abilities. Specifically, they have spell abilities, which are the instructions that are followed when the spell resolves. For example, an instant or sorcery spell's text is a spell ability unless it is an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the criteria in rule 113.6. Additionally, some static abilities of instant or sorcery spells function while the spell is on the stack, such as those that affect how the spell can be cast or countered. However, non-permanent spells do not have abilities that function on the battlefield, as they are not permanents. This is supported by rules [113.3a] and [113.6].

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Rule [702.61b] explicitly states that players may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. This is an exception to the general restriction in [702.61a] that prevents players from casting other spells or activating non-mana abilities. Mana abilities, as defined in [605.1] and [605.3a], can be activated whenever a player has priority or needs to pay mana, and they resolve immediately without using the stack ([605.3b], [405.6c]). Therefore, you are free to activate mana abilities during the resolution of a spell with split second, such as tapping lands for mana or using other mana-producing abilities.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: Counterspell resolves first, and Divination does not resolve. When all players pass priority, the top object on the stack—Counterspell—resolves (rule 117.4). Counterspell's effect counters target spell, which removes Divination from the stack (rule 701.6a). Since Divination is countered, it never resolves and none of its effects occur (rule 701.6a). After Counterspell finishes resolving, it is put into its owner's graveyard (rule 608.2n). Divination is already removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard as part of being countered (rule 701.6a).

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 1 damage to Vampire Nighthawk before any excess damage can trample over to the defending player. Because Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any nonzero amount of combat damage from a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for trample assignment purposes. Since Charging Rhino has trample, you first assign lethal damage to the blocking creature (Vampire Nighthawk). Under rule 702.2c, any nonzero amount of damage from a deathtouch source is lethal, so you need only assign 1 damage to Vampire Nighthawk. The remaining 3 damage from Charging Rhino's 4 power can be assigned to the defending player. This is true regardless of Vampire Nighthawk's actual toughness of 3, because the deathtouch rule overrides the normal lethal damage calculation for trample assignment. The answer is the same in both two-player and multiplayer games, as the trample and deathtouch rules do not differ based on player count.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers before the cascaded spell resolves. Here's the detailed reasoning:

When you cast Shardless Agent, its cascade ability triggers and goes on the stack above Shardless Agent itself. Cascade resolves first, exiling cards until a nonland card with lesser mana value is exiled, and you may cast that card without paying its mana cost. If that card is a noncreature spell, casting it causes Monastery Swiftspear's prowess to trigger. Per [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2], prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger, meaning it will resolve before that cascaded spell. This is consistent with the general rule that triggered abilities from casting a spell resolve before the spell itself (see [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #0]). The cascaded spell is cast during the resolution of cascade, so prowess triggers immediately upon that casting and is put onto the stack above the cascaded spell, ensuring prowess resolves first.

This answer assumes the cascaded spell is a noncreature spell (e.g., an instant or sorcery). If the cascaded spell were a creature spell, prowess would not trigger at all per [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1]. The timing is unambiguous because cascade resolves before Shardless Agent, and the cascaded spell is cast during that resolution.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: No, state-based actions do not make the Grizzly Bears die before Lightning Bolt resolves. State-based actions are only checked before a player would receive priority (rule 117.5), not during the resolution of a spell. Lightning Bolt resolves as a single event (rule 608.1), and state-based actions are not checked in the middle of that resolution (rule 704.4). After Lightning Bolt finishes resolving, the Grizzly Bears will have 3 damage marked on it (the original 2 plus the 3 from Lightning Bolt), which is lethal damage (rule 120.6). State-based actions will then destroy the Grizzly Bears as a state-based action the next time they are checked, which is before any player receives priority (rule 117.5). The damage from Lightning Bolt is marked on the creature during step three of the damage process (rule 120.4c), and the creature is not destroyed until state-based actions are performed afterward. If the question instead meant whether the Grizzly Bears dies after Lightning Bolt resolves, the answer is yes—it will be destroyed as a state-based action before any player gets priority.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text: The triggers both go on the stack during the upkeep step, before any player gets priority. The order is chosen by the active player (the player whose turn it is) first, then the nonactive player, following APNAP order. Specifically, the active player puts all triggered abilities they control on the stack in any order they choose, then the nonactive player does the same. Since Phyrexian Arena's ability triggers at the beginning of your upkeep, and your opponent's ability also triggers at the beginning of your upkeep (assuming it's a beginning-of-upkeep trigger), both trigger simultaneously when the upkeep step begins, per rule [500.6]. They are put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is at the start of the upkeep step after any turn-based actions (none in upkeep) and before the active player gets priority, per [503.1a] and [117.3a]. The order of placement is determined by [603.3b]: first, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose. Since both triggers have the same trigger condition (beginning of upkeep), they are both placed in this first part. The active player (you, since it's your turn) chooses the order for your Phyrexian Arena's trigger and any other triggers you control, then the nonactive player (your opponent) chooses the order for their triggers. If there are only these two triggers, you choose whether your Phyrexian Arena's trigger goes on the stack above or below your opponent's trigger, and then your opponent does the same for their trigger. The result is that the trigger placed last (on top of the stack) will resolve first. This answer assumes a two-player game. In a multiplayer game with more than two players, the same APNAP order applies: the active player puts all their triggers on the stack in any order, then each nonactive player in turn order does the same, per [603.3b]. If the game uses teams (e.g., Two-Headed Giant), rule [805.4d] and [805.7] apply, where each team takes turns and the active team puts all their triggers on the stack first, then each nonactive team in turn order.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: Zero copies of the card end up in your hand. The original sorcery with buyback returns to your hand because you paid the buyback cost. The copy created by Fork is not a card—it is a copy of a spell on the stack with no associated card—so it cannot be returned to your hand by buyback or any other effect. After Fork resolves, the Fork card goes to the graveyard, and the copy remains on the stack until it resolves, then ceases to exist (it is not put into any zone).

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. When the face-down manifested Lightning Bolt dies, Mimic Vat's triggered ability exiles that card. However, Lightning Bolt is an instant card, not a permanent card. Mimic Vat's activated ability creates a token that is a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat, but [Mimic Vat ruling #0] explicitly states: "If the creature that dies is an instant or sorcery card that's been manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled. You can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card. No token is created in this case." Since Lightning Bolt is an instant (a nonpermanent card), the copy ability will fail to create a token. This is consistent with [111.12], which says if an effect instructs a player to create a token that is a copy of a nonexistent object, no token is created — here, the object exists but is not a valid type for token creation under Mimic Vat's ability. The answer is the same regardless of the number of players, as this interaction does not depend on player count.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. The two abilities on Fiend Hunter are linked abilities: the first exiles a creature, and the second refers to “the exiled card.” When you copy the first ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is also linked to the same second ability. Because the second ability now refers to multiple exiled cards (the one from the original ability and the one from the copy), when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, the second ability returns each of those exiled cards to the battlefield under their owner’s control. This is confirmed by Lithoform Engine ruling #4, which states that if an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability are also linked to that second ability, and if the second ability refers to “the exiled card,” it refers to all cards exiled by the first ability and the copy. Rule 607.3 further explains that when a linked ability refers to “the exiled card” and multiple cards have been exiled, the ability performs its action on each exiled card. The answer assumes the copy resolves and exiles the second creature before Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield; if Fiend Hunter leaves before the copy resolves, the second creature would not be exiled and only the first would return (per Fiend Hunter ruling #0).

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. When Banishing Light phases out due to Teferi's Protection, the delayed one-shot effect that would return the exiled creature "until Banishing Light leaves the battlefield" does not happen. This is because phasing out is not the same as leaving the battlefield, and the game treats phased-out permanents as though they don't exist for most purposes, but the "until" effect is not triggered by phasing out. Specifically, Teferi's Protection ruling #21 states: "Any one-shot effects that are waiting 'until [this] leaves the battlefield,' such as that of Banishing Light, won't happen when a permanent phases out." Additionally, rule [702.26d] confirms that phasing does not cause zone-change triggers, so Banishing Light's own "leaves the battlefield" ability does not trigger. The exiled creature remains in exile indefinitely until Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield (e.g., by being destroyed, exiled, or returned to hand) or until some other effect returns it. The answer is the same in both two-player and multiplayer games, as the relevant rules and rulings do not differ based on player count for this interaction.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
No, your opponent cannot target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell, and if they somehow could, you would still control their next turn. 

**Reasoning:**

1. **Protection from instants applies only on the battlefield, not on the stack.** Emrakul, the Promised End has protection from instants, but according to [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2], protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield. While Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack (as a spell), it does not have protection from instants. Therefore, your opponent can legally target it with Counterspell while it is on the stack. 

2. **The cast trigger resolves independently of whether Emrakul, the Promised End is countered.** The triggered ability from Emrakul, the Promised End ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.") goes on the stack when you cast it. Even if Counterspell counters Emrakul, the Promised End, the triggered ability is already on the stack and will resolve normally. Rule [603.10e] confirms that abilities that trigger when a spell is countered look back in time, but here the trigger is from casting, not from being countered. The trigger resolves, and you will gain control of the targeted opponent during their next turn, and after that turn, they take an extra turn. 

3. **If Counterspell were to counter Emrakul, the Promised End, the triggered ability still resolves.** The triggered ability is separate from the spell itself. Rule [113.9] states that triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells and can't be countered by effects that counter only spells (like Counterspell). So even if Emrakul, the Promised End is countered, the triggered ability remains on the stack and resolves, giving you control of the opponent's next turn and the extra turn. 

**Assumption about timing:** The question assumes the opponent responds to the cast trigger with Counterspell. This is the standard order: you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its cast trigger goes on the stack, then your opponent can respond with Counterspell targeting the Emrakul spell. If the opponent instead tried to Counterspell before the trigger resolves, the above still applies. If the opponent waited until after the trigger resolved, the Emrakul spell would still be on the stack and could be countered, but the trigger would have already resolved. 

**Two-player vs. multiplayer:** The provided rules do not contain specific multiplayer rules for this interaction. The answer above applies to a two-player game. In a multiplayer game, the same rules apply, but the targeted opponent is chosen from among all opponents. The effect still works as described. 

**Key definitions:** 
- **Protection from instants** (from [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1]): Emrakul can't be targeted by instant spells or activated/triggered abilities from instant cards, and damage from such sources is prevented. But this only applies while Emrakul is on the battlefield, per [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]. 
- **Cast trigger**: A triggered ability that triggers when a spell is cast, as per [603.1a]. It goes on the stack and resolves independently of the spell. 
- **Countering a spell**: Counterspell targets a spell on the stack and removes it, putting it into the graveyard per [608.2n].

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
No, you cannot cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor via cascade from a spell with mana value less than 7. Cascade checks the mana value of the card you exile, and for a double-faced card, its mana value is always calculated using the mana cost of its front face, regardless of which face is up. Valki, God of Lies has a mana value of 2 (from its front face cost {1}{B}). Cascade requires the exiled nonland card to have a mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value. If your cascade spell's mana value is, say, 5, then Valki, God of Lies (MV 2) is a legal hit because 2 < 5. However, when you cast the card, you may only cast it using its front face (Valki, God of Lies) by default, unless an effect specifically allows you to cast it "transformed" or "converted." Cascade does not provide such an effect. Therefore, you cannot cast the back face Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor via cascade. You could cast Valki, God of Lies for free if its mana value (2) is less than the cascade spell's mana value, but not Tibalt.

**Reasoning:**
- Rule [702.85a] defines cascade: you exile cards until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than this spell's mana value, and you may cast that card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell's mana value is less than this spell's mana value.
- Rule [712.8c] states that for a nonmodal double-faced card (which Valki/Tibalt is, as a modal double-faced card? Actually, Valki/Tibalt is a modal double-faced card, not nonmodal. However, the provided rules do not include a specific rule for modal double-faced cards' mana value calculation. Rule [712.8c] explicitly covers nonmodal double-faced cards, stating "its mana value is calculated using the mana cost of its front face." For modal double-faced cards, the same principle applies per the card's own rulings: [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14] says to consider only the characteristics of the face you're playing, and the mana value is derived from the front face's mana cost. The card's Oracle text confirms Valki's mana value is 2.
- Rule [712.11c] says a double-faced spell is cast with its front face up by default. Rule [712.11d] allows casting "transformed" only if an ability of the front face allows it. Cascade does not grant such an ability.
- Therefore, the only legal cast from the cascade trigger is the front face, Valki, God of Lies, not Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor.

**Assumption:** The question assumes the cascade spell's mana value is greater than 2 (e.g., 5 or more). If the cascade spell's mana value were 1 or less, Valki (MV 2) would not be a legal hit because 2 is not less than 1, and the cascade would continue exiling. The answer does not change regarding Tibalt: it is never castable via cascade unless an effect specifically allows casting the back face.

**Multiplayer note:** The provided rules do not contain multiplayer-specific cascade rules. The answer is the same for any number of players because cascade's condition depends only on mana values, not on player count.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control one of your opponent's turns (the one from the original Emrakul, the Promised End's cast trigger), you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End token, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell with Lithoform Engine does NOT give you another control-a-turn trigger.

**Reasoning:**

1. **Copying the cast trigger with Lithoform Engine:** The first activation of Lithoform Engine copies the triggered ability "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." Per [Lithoform Engine ruling #3], this creates another instance of that ability on the stack. Per [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14], multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other; the last one to be created is the one that works. Since both the original and the copy target the same opponent, the copy (being the last created) will determine the control effect. However, the extra turn from the original trigger still exists. The copy's effect says "After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." So you control the opponent's next turn (from the copy), and after that turn, the opponent takes an extra turn (from the original trigger). The copy's extra turn is redundant because the original already gave one, but the control effect is overwritten by the copy. So you control one turn, and the opponent gets one extra turn after that.

2. **Copying the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell:** The second activation of Lithoform Engine (after untapping with Voltaic Key) copies the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack. Per [Lithoform Engine ruling #5], this creates a copy of the permanent spell on the stack. Per [111.13], a copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. So you get a token copy of Emrakul, the Promised End. This token is a second Emrakul on the battlefield.

3. **Does copying the Emrakul spell give another control-a-turn trigger?** No. The "When you cast this spell" trigger only triggers when you *cast* Emrakul, the Promised End. Per [707.10e], a copy of a spell is not cast. The copy created by Lithoform Engine is put directly onto the stack without being cast, so the cast trigger does not trigger again. You only get the one cast trigger from the original casting.

**Assumptions about timing:** This assumes you activate Lithoform Engine's first ability (to copy the trigger) while the cast trigger is on the stack, then untap Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key and activate its third ability (to copy the permanent spell) while the original Emrakul spell is still on the stack. If you did the permanent spell copy first, the result would be the same regarding the cast trigger (it still doesn't trigger from the copy). The order of the two Lithoform Engine activations does not affect the number of control-a-turn triggers.

**Multiplayer note:** The provided rules do not contain specific multiplayer rules for extra turns beyond the shared team turns option (rule 805.8) and Grand Melee (rule 807.4). In a standard multiplayer game (not using those variants), the answer is the same: you control one opponent's turn, and that opponent gets one extra turn after the turn you control. The extra turn is added per [500.7] in APNAP order if multiple extra turns are created.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you get two tokens. When the original Mimic Vat ability resolves, it creates one token copy of the exiled card. The copy of that ability created by Lithoform Engine also resolves and creates a second token copy of the exiled card. The two tokens are created independently, and each is a separate token. The fact that the original ability was copied does not prevent the copy from creating a token, as long as a card is still exiled with Mimic Vat when each ability resolves. The copy of the ability is a separate instance on the stack and follows the same rules as the original ability (rule 707.10e). The token created by the copy is not “created” for the purposes of replacement effects that refer to creating a token, per Lithoform Engine ruling #15, but that does not affect the number of tokens you get—you still get two tokens. The order of resolution does not matter; both abilities will create a token as long as the exiled card remains. If the exiled card is somehow removed before one of the abilities resolves, that ability will not create a token (Mimic Vat ruling #6).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, its total cost is {G}{G} (two green mana). You get zero Forest Dryad tokens because X=0. You should actually choose X=1, which makes the total cost {1}{G}{G} (one generic and two green mana), and you get one Forest Dryad token. Here is the reasoning step by step.

First, define the key terms. Awaken the Woods has a mana cost of {X}{G}{G}. The value of X is chosen by you as you cast the spell (rule 107.3a). The total cost is determined by starting with the mana cost, applying any cost reductions, then applying Trinisphere's effect (Trinisphere ruling #0). The permanent that makes your green spells cost {1} less reduces the generic component of the cost by {1} (it does not affect the colored symbols).

**Case 1: X=0**
- Mana cost: {0}{G}{G} = {G}{G}.
- Cost reduction: {1} less, so {G}{G} becomes {G}{G} (cannot go below {0}; rule 601.2f says the mana component cannot be reduced below {0}, and here it is already {0} generic, so reduction has no effect).
- Mana component before Trinisphere: {0} (since the cost is {G}{G}, the generic part is 0).
- Trinisphere effect: If the mana component is less than 3, it becomes 3. So the mana component becomes {3}, and the total cost becomes {3}{G}{G}.
- However, rule 107.3b applies: if you cast a spell with {X} in its mana cost, the value of X is not defined by the spell's text, and an effect lets you cast it while paying neither its mana cost nor an alternative cost that includes X, then the only legal choice for X is 0. But here you are paying the mana cost (not an alternative cost), so 107.3b does not apply. You may choose X=0.
- Result: Total cost {3}{G}{G}. You get zero tokens (since X=0).

**Case 2: X=1**
- Mana cost: {1}{G}{G}.
- Cost reduction: {1} less, so {1}{G}{G} becomes {0}{G}{G} = {G}{G}.
- Mana component before Trinisphere: {0} (since the cost is {G}{G}, generic part is 0).
- Trinisphere effect: Mana component becomes {3}, so total cost becomes {3}{G}{G}.
- Result: Total cost {3}{G}{G}. You get one token (since X=1).

**Comparison:**
- X=0: cost {3}{G}{G}, get 0 tokens.
- X=1: cost {3}{G}{G}, get 1 token.
- X=2: cost {3}{G}{G} (since {2}{G}{G} reduced to {1}{G}{G}, mana component 1, Trinisphere raises to 3, total {3}{G}{G}), get 2 tokens.
- In general, for any X >= 1, the total cost is {3}{G}{G} because the cost reduction and Trinisphere interact to always make the mana component 3. So you should choose the highest X you want (subject to mana availability) because the cost is fixed at {3}{G}{G} for any X >= 1. The optimal choice depends on how many tokens you want; if you only want one token, X=1 is fine. If you want more, choose a higher X.

**Important note:** This answer assumes a two-player game. In a multiplayer game, the same rules apply; Trinisphere's effect is not player-specific, so the cost calculation is identical regardless of number of opponents.

**Timing assumption:** The cost reduction and Trinisphere are both static effects that apply during the cost determination step of casting the spell (rule 601.2f). There is no ambiguity about order because Trinisphere ruling #0 specifies the order: start with mana cost, add cost increases, apply cost reductions, then apply Trinisphere. The answer would not change under any other timing because the rules mandate this order.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard with Animate Dead. When Animate Dead's triggered ability resolves, it returns the enchanted creature card (Grist, the Hunger Tide) to the battlefield under your control. However, because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a planeswalker, once it enters the battlefield it is no longer a creature (per [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]), and Animate Dead's enchant ability changes to "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura." Since Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature on the battlefield, Animate Dead cannot legally be attached to it. As a result, Animate Dead will be put into the graveyard as a state-based action (per [Animate Dead ruling #4]), which triggers its delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it"). When that trigger resolves, you will sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide. So Grist, the Hunger Tide will briefly be on the battlefield, then be sacrificed. Note that if Grist, the Hunger Tide has protection from black or another reason it can't be enchanted, the same outcome occurs: Animate Dead can't attach, goes to graveyard, and Grist is sacrificed. This answer assumes the two-player case; in multiplayer, the same rules apply but "that creature's controller" refers to the player who controlled Grist when Animate Dead left the battlefield.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Skullbriar, the Walking Grave will not keep its four +1/+1 counters when it is recast from the command zone, and Doubling Season will not double any counters as it enters the battlefield because it enters without any counters.

**Reasoning:**
- When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies and you move it to the command zone, it changes zones (from battlefield to graveyard, then from graveyard to command zone). Rule [122.2] states that counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another; the counters simply cease to exist. However, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has a card ability that says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." This card text overrides the general rule [122.2] for zone changes to the graveyard and command zone, so the counters remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave while it is in the graveyard and when it moves to the command zone.
- When you recast Skullbriar, the Walking Grave from the command zone, it moves from the command zone to the stack (as a spell), then from the stack to the battlefield (as a permanent). Rule [400.7] says an object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of its previous existence. The card's ability only retains counters when moving to zones other than a player's hand or library, but moving from the command zone to the stack and then to the battlefield is a zone change. The counters that were on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave in the command zone cease to exist when it leaves the command zone (rule [122.2] applies again, and the card's exception does not cover moving from command zone to stack/battlefield). Therefore, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave enters the battlefield as a new object with no counters.
- Doubling Season's second ability says: "If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many of those counters on that permanent instead." Since Skullbriar, the Walking Grave enters the battlefield without any counters being put on it by an effect (it simply enters as a 1/1 creature with no counters), Doubling Season does not apply. There is no effect putting counters on it as it enters.

**Assumption:** The question assumes Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies, you move it to the command zone via the state-based action in rule [903.9a], and then you cast it from the command zone. The timing is clear: the counters are present in the command zone but are lost upon leaving that zone to be cast.

**Multiplayer note:** The answer is the same for any number of players, as the relevant rules (zone changes, counters, and Doubling Season) are not player-count dependent.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. Final Fortune's delayed triggered ability triggers at the beginning of the extra turn's end step. Because Sundial of the Infinite's activated ability ends the turn before the end step begins, the end step is skipped entirely, so the delayed trigger never triggers and you never lose the game. This is confirmed by Final Fortune's ruling: "If you end up skipping the extra turn that is gained, you do not lose the game." The same logic applies when the end step itself is skipped. Sundial of the Infinite's ruling also states that if its ability is activated before the end step, any "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities won't get the chance to trigger that turn because the end step is skipped. The turn ends during the current phase (here, presumably a main phase or combat), and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping the end step entirely. Since the delayed trigger never goes on the stack, you do not lose the game. This answer assumes you activate Sundial of the Infinite during the extra turn granted by Final Fortune, before the end step of that turn begins. If you activated it after the end step had already started, the trigger would already be on the stack and you would lose when it resolves, but the question states "before the end step," so that timing is not at issue.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, and no player can respond to that choice because it is made during the resolution of the spell that puts Clone onto the battlefield. Specifically, Clone's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield (see [707.5]). You make the choice when the replacement effect is applied, which happens as Clone enters the battlefield, not when Clone is cast or when it is on the stack. Since the choice is made during the resolution of the spell (the moment Clone enters), there is no round of priority between the choice and Clone entering; opponents cannot respond to the choice itself. If you choose not to copy anything, Clone enters as a 0/0 and is put into the graveyard immediately (see [Clone ruling #5]).

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get zero lands from that one Flooded Strand. Flooded Strand's activated ability is a mana ability (it produces mana by putting a land onto the battlefield, and it doesn't target), and Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability explicitly states "Mana abilities can't be targeted." Therefore, Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability cannot target Flooded Strand's ability on the stack, so no copies are created and only the original Flooded Strand ability resolves, giving you one land. The question asks about copies from Gogo, Master of Mimicry, so the answer is zero lands from those copies.

Reasoning: Flooded Strand's ability is a mana ability because it is an activated ability that doesn't target and could produce mana (by putting a land onto the battlefield, which is a mana-producing permanent). Rule [106.7] defines how to determine what mana a permanent could produce, and Flooded Strand's ability puts a Plains or Island onto the battlefield, which are lands that could produce mana. Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability has the restriction "Mana abilities can't be targeted" in its own text, which overrides any general rules about targeting. Since the target is illegal, the ability doesn't create any copies. The original Flooded Strand ability still resolves normally, giving you one land.

This answer assumes the timing is as stated: you activate Flooded Strand's ability first, then activate Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability targeting it. If the order were reversed (Gogo's ability activated first, then Flooded Strand's), the result would be the same because Gogo's ability can't target a mana ability at all.
